pages.alt: Cover. A honey-gold crescent moon with a gentle face and a sleeping cloud float over white lilies and an ornamental butterfly on a deep indigo night.
All twenty-eight phases of the moon arc across the night sky above a garden of lilies, with a sleeping cloud at the left.
A cast sheet of the book's living pieces: moon faces through their phases, ornamental butterflies, clouds that are happy, sleeping, and raining, and a border of flowers.
An open book rests in a moonlit garden, holding a crown, a lantern, a ship's wheel, a small blue book and a butterfly, while three moon faces drift above it.
The mother in her long indigo robe holds her small daughter's hand and they walk together toward a closed book, a crescent moon above and a butterfly nearby.

content.title: Two more things, and then we begin.
body: On the twenty-ninth night, this book will send you outside. Dress warmly. Take a tall hand with you.
And there is one page in here that stays closed… the rarest story, which only the sky can unlock, and only on the months that run long. Do not peek. It knows.
That is everything. The moon is already rising, and she does not like to be kept waiting by anyone except you.

pages.alt: Section title: The First Stories, from before anyone counted nights. A small crescent moon with a face and a butterfly rest among lilies on cream.
The Butterfly and the Moon. A butterfly lifts from a white lily as a thread of light crosses to a crescent moon on the right of the spread.
The Story Hour. In the grey hour just before morning, the crescent moon leans low over a sleeping garden while a butterfly rests among giant lilies.
Why the Moon Changes Shape. A row of moon faces shrinks from full to crescent across the sky, giving pieces of light away to the stars.
The Butterfly's Colors. A large ornamental butterfly glows above a sunrise-tinted garden, its wings coloured by the moon before the dew ever flew.
The Moon's Favorite. A great full moon with a serene face smiles near morning while small stars climb toward it down beams of light.

pages.alt: Week One divider. A honey-gold crescent moon with a face hangs in a deep blue sky above a lantern, a candle, a loaf of bread and a butterfly among the flowers.

pages.eyebrow: Week Two · First Quarter · The Powerful Forms
pages.alt: Week Two divider. A growing half-moon with a calm face rises over a crown, a compass, a ship, a white tigress and a star among deep-blue waves. This week the small one's work is admiring, and imitating.

pages.eyebrow: Week Three · Full Moon · The Mirror
pages.alt: Week Three divider. A full moon shines through a tall window while a mother and her daughter stand before a mirror and both their faces can be seen. This week the light is at its fullest.

pages.eyebrow: Week Four · Waning · The Passing Down
pages.alt: Week Four divider. A waning moon hangs in the window as the mother pours a stream of golden light down into her small daughter's cupped hands, a lantern glowing beside them. This week the light travels; watch where it goes.

pages.eyebrow: Night One · The Cloud Who Chose a Garden
pages.alt: Night One, The Cloud Who Chose a Garden. A small cloud settles low over a child asleep in a moonlit garden, keeping her in cool shade while other clouds race high above.

content.title: The Cloud Who Chose a Garden
body: The big clouds raced across the sky, as big clouds do.
They wanted to be everywhere. They wanted to be seen by whole cities. They thundered so nobody would forget them.
But one small, fluffy cloud stopped, right over one small garden, and stayed.
“The sky is enormous!” the big clouds called down. “Why would you stay there?”
The little cloud did not answer the big clouds. She was busy.
Because in that garden, every day at noon, someone very small took her nap in the grass. The sun at noon is strong, and small sleepers are precious.
So the cloud spread herself out, soft and wide, like a blanket hung in the sky.
And the small sleeper slept in the coolest shade in the whole city. She never knew why, and never got burned, not once, not ever.
A girl who watches the sky will tell you clouds never stay.
content.coda: The softest ones choose one garden, and guard one nap, and call it enough.
